prize_parts.citation: for credible empirical analysis of how technology and international trade shocks reshape labour demand, wages and local labour-market adjustment

statement.case_for: B037 remains my preferred achievement, but my configuration has changed: I now name Dorn instead of Katz. On the chair's question, I treat the achievement as one discovery, defined narrowly. It is design-based evidence on how technology and trade shocks change labour demand and local adjustment, with Autor linking the task view of work to the import-competition evidence. That evidence combines new data, transparent quasi-experimental designs and an explanatory frame. It addresses a large and hard question, it has been replicated in other countries, and it has run for over a decade, long enough to be qualified without being overturned. I changed Katz to Dorn for two reasons. First, the import-shock papers are a jointly authored body of work, and omitting Dorn would misstate where the evidence came from. Second, the incremental contribution of Katz's strand is the long-run education-versus-technology account of the skill premium. That is the part closest to ground already recognised in 2023, so it is where a new prize adds least. The trio adds the least-overlapping empirical contribution. I do not claim that Katz's work is less important, and I do not rely on support counts as evidence of merit. I would keep the citation to what these three developed and not claim the task framework as their origination.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the narrower trio leaves out the long-run skill-premium and education-technology framework. That framework gives the trade evidence its general meaning, and omitting Katz is a real attribution cost. The task framework also owes much to Acemoglu, Levy and Murnane, who are outside the credited set, so the citation cannot claim it. The magnitude and persistence of the China-shock effects and the robustness of shift-share designs are still debated. If the committee judges the technology and trade strands to be separate discoveries, this prize rests on the trade strand alone and has a thinner conceptual part. In that case a candidate with cleaner single-discovery attribution, such as B001, becomes a serious competitor on attribution grounds. I also changed my view after weighing the Goldin overlap more heavily than I did in round 1. I cannot fully separate that judgement from having presented the 2023 prize.

responses.point: Hassler moved to Autor, Dorn and Hanson because Katz's skill-premium work sits close to ground recognised in 2023 and 2024, and Dorn co-authored the least-overlapping empirical contribution. He concedes that this leaves out the long-run education-versus-technology framing and says the committee should weigh that openly.
responses.response: This is the argument that moved me. In round 1 I said the overlap with Goldin's prize was partial and kept Katz so that both strands were credited. I still think the overlap should not be overstated, but his point about what each name adds is the better test. Dorn adds identified evidence that no earlier prize covers. Katz would add a framing that is adjacent to recognised work. I agree with his caution that the cost should be stated and not hidden, so my citation does not claim the skill-premium or task framework. I also accept his point that Autor carries the task and polarisation strand, so the technology side is not left unattributed.

responses.point: Fredriksson keeps Katz because the achievement is about technology and trade together. Dropping Katz would leave the technology side resting on Autor alone, since Katz-Murphy and Autor-Katz-Krueger supply the demand-supply framing of the skill premium. He accepts a Dorn trio on scientific grounds if the committee prefers a narrower prize.
responses.response: I take this seriously, and it is the best case against my change. My answer is that the citation can honour the technology side through Autor, whose work spans the task and trade evidence, without the framing being credited to the trio as a whole. A narrower prize built on one object, the demand for labour under technology and trade shocks, is easier to defend than a composite one. If the committee concludes the two strands are one discovery and wants both honoured, the Katz variant is legitimate. I would not oppose it on scientific grounds, and I have not resolved this cleanly.

responses.point: Boppart asks the committee to decide whether B037 is one discovery or two before it takes precedence over a pair whose joint credit is unambiguous. He regards it as the most serious competitor to B001 if it is judged coherent, and notes that the size of the trade-shock effects is still debated.
responses.response: I answer his question by narrowing the claim, which is the reason for the change. The trio's discovery is design-based evidence on adjustment to technology and trade shocks, and the citation does not extend to the whole skill-premium history. On that definition the credit is coherent and jointly authored. I accept the debate over magnitudes. I read it as the sign of a mature, scrutinised programme and not a reason to wait, which is why the citation says 'credible empirical analysis' and not a settled welfare verdict. I still weigh B001's clean two-name attribution as a real advantage. I have moved it up to be my first listed alternative, in part because of his argument. I defer to the macroeconomists on the framework's theoretical importance, and the unresolved disconnect puzzles remain my reason for not placing it first.

responses.point: Dreber adopted Autor, Dorn and Hanson because the import-shock papers are a coherent body of work. She words the citation around credibly identified evidence and not the whole skill-premium history. She also says B038 is better left to a later round because its causal neighbourhood-effect findings have had less time for independent replication.
responses.response: I agree on the trio and on the wording, and I have adopted both. On B038 I accept her replication point and have taken it out of my alternatives, even though I ranked it third in my opening. Its findings are important, but independent replication and long-run follow-up are thinner than for the B037 and B001 literatures. I would not credit it ahead of candidates whose designs have been tested more often.

uncertainties: Whether the committee treats the technology and trade-shock strands as one discovery or two, and whether a prize honouring only the trade-shock design would be seen as too narrow.

Whether my weight on the overlap between Katz's skill-premium strand and the Goldin prize is right. Others judge the overlap to be only thematic, and my 2023 presentation role may bias me in either direction.
How persistent and how large the China-shock effects were, and how robust shift-share identification and task measures are.
How much credit for the task framework belongs to authors outside the credited names (Acemoglu, Levy, Murnane), which limits what the citation can claim.

My comparative judgement on B001 and B013 relies on macroeconomists' arguments because those are outside my research area. I have not independently verified any sources and rely on my own recollection of the literature.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. It lists no co-authorship or institutional tie to Autor, Dorn or Hanson, nor to Katz, and the frequent co-authors it names are not on B037. I presented the 2023 prize (Goldin) at the announcement. That work is adjacent to Katz's earlier collaboration with Goldin and is part of my reasoning for the change to Dorn, so I disclose it. I also work in labour economics, which is close to B037, and I have tried to apply the same criteria as for other fields. These are disclosures, not adjudicated.
